newsitem.title: USA: FCOJ futures continue to sink on record Fla. crop.
newsitem.headline: FCOJ futures continue to sink on record Fla. crop.

text.p: FCOJ futures sunk to fresh four-year lows on Friday, as speculators continued to sell heavily amid the prospect of another record crop in Florida, traders said.

Industry sources said speculators were following through on a sharp sell-off on Thursday, when the benchmark September contract plunged by more than 12 percent after a private forecaster Citrus Consulting International of Orlando, Fla. pegged the 1997/98 Florida orange juice crop at a record 253 million 90-lb boxes.
An estimated 253 million-box crop would be a hefty 12 percent increase over Florida's 1996/97 crop of a record 225.7 million boxes.

"Two hundred and fifty-three is a big number," said Allendale Commodities analyst Jim Cordier. "For the most part, this market is terminal now. It is not going to be able to shake this number for awhile."

Friday, September juice fell to a new life-of-contract low of 67.50 cents per lb, before trade buying emerged to trim losses, dealers said. At the close, September stood at 68.90 cents, down 0.75 cent.
The rest of the board was trading the daily 5.00 cent limit lower to 4.70 cents lower, and all contracts had hit new lifetime lows.
Some traders and analysts predicted the recent sell-off in juice futures is only the beginning of a long-term downtrend that could push the market below 60.00 cents.

"The fact is, we've never had a situation where there are record ending stocks anticipated by a record crop when retail prices remain relatively high and Brazil is having record output," Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said. "Plus, the specs are heavily long."
The most recent weekly spec/hedge report put out by the exchange showed speculators were 77.7 percent long the market as of August 8.

"The speculative commitment in the market is in excess of 77 percent," Jimmy Quinn, a floor source with AG Edwards, said. "With the specs long before the report and the report coming out negative, there is quite a bit of liquidation that needs to be done before the market turns around."
Technically, traders pegged September chart support at 65.45 cents, the low hit in 1993. The next downside target seen at 60.00 cents.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture will release its first estimate of the 1997/98 crop in October.
